conventions: stop entries mechanized as signal-bar-close then next-bar-open; every tunable constant is a parameter; long side only in pseudocode

candidates.name: ThreePushWedgePattern
candidates.quote: it has at least five legs, but unlike a typical triangle, the second leg often exceeds the prior swing point... three countertrend pushes, which is all that is needed to qualify as a triangle, or, if it is sloping, a wedge type of triangle, or simply a wedge.
candidates.description: A wedge is a countertrend move of at least three swing pushes (each push a local extreme against the prevailing direction), typically contained between a converging (or parallel) trend line and trend channel line. Shared primitive: other wedge candidates in this chapter depend on it.
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (pattern classification used as a signal precondition)

complexity.reason: needs swing-pivot detection, a running push count across pivots, and trend-line/channel-line convergence from those pivots

notes: Brooks does not give a strict push count; 3 is the stated minimum ('all that is needed to qualify'), kept as a tunable in case a stricter count is wanted.
This is the chapter's core shared primitive; wedge-flag vs wedge-reversal distinction and slope-based bias (R18-09) both build on it.

candidates.name: WedgePullbackWithTrendEntry
candidates.quote: A wedge pullback is a with-trend setup, and traders can enter on the first signal, as soon as the market reverses back into the direction of the trend.
candidates.description: In an established trend, once a wedge pullback (three-push countertrend move) completes, enter with-trend on the first reversal signal bar back in the trend direction.
candidates.book_order_type: buy stop one tick above the signal bar's high

complexity.reason: inherits R18-01's pivot/convergence detection and additionally needs an established-trend context filter (defined elsewhere in the corpus)

notes: Also depends conceptually on a 'bull/bear trend context' primitive that this chapter does not itself define; likely already mined in the Trends book chapters.

candidates.name: WedgeReversalSecondEntryFilter
candidates.quote: unlike a wedge pullback, a wedge reversal is a countertrend setup and it is therefore usually better to wait for a second entry... unless a wedge top is extremely strong, traders should wait for the bear breakout and then assess its strength.
candidates.description: When a wedge forms as a countertrend reversal pattern (not a with-trend pullback), skip the first breakout entry and wait for a second entry (e.g., a breakout pullback) unless the wedge is extremely strong.
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (gates whether to act on the first vs second breakout signal)

complexity.reason: 'extremely strong' is a discretionary judgment call with no stated bar-level test; a design decision (e.g., trend-bar count, overlap, momentum score) is needed before this can be coded

candidates.name: WedgeFlagDurationFilter
candidates.quote: wedge flags are usually smaller patterns and most last about 10 to 20 bars.
candidates.description: A with-trend wedge flag is typically 10 to 20 bars long from its first push to its completion; treat wedges outside this range as less typical.
candidates.pseudocode:
wedgeDurationBars = currentBarIndex - wedgeStartBarIndex; // bars since the wedge's first push began
isTypicalWedgeFlagLength = wedgeDurationBars >= minWedgeBars && wedgeDurationBars <= maxWedgeBars;

complexity.reason: needs a persistent counter from the wedge's identified start bar (itself dependent on R18-01's pivot detection), but the count/compare itself is simple cross-bar state

candidates.name: ReversalPatternMinDurationFilter
candidates.quote: A reversal usually needs to be at least 20 bars long and have a clear trend channel line to be strong enough to reverse a trend.
candidates.description: A reversal pattern (as opposed to a with-trend wedge pullback) is only considered strong enough to reverse the trend if it has lasted at least N bars and has a clear trend channel line.

complexity.reason: requires trend-channel-line projection from pivots plus a persistent bar counter from the pattern's identified start

notes: 'Clear trend channel line' has no numeric definition; minChannelFitQuality is a placeholder for whatever line-fit quality measure the authoring pass adopts.

candidates.name: NoBuyOnGapAboveSignalBar
candidates.quote: don't buy on the gap up; take an entry only if the entry bar opens below the high of the signal bar and then trades through your buy stop
candidates.description: For a with-trend buy-stop entry above a signal bar's high, only take the entry if the entry bar's open is below the signal bar's high (no gap up through the stop); if the market gaps above the signal bar's high, skip that entry.
candidates.pseudocode: isValidLongStopEntry = open[0] < (high[1] + entryTick) && high[0] >= (high[1] + entryTick); // bar[1] is the signal bar; buy stop sits entryTick above its high
candidates.book_order_type: buy stop one tick above the signal bar's high, canceled/skipped if the open gaps through it

complexity.reason: a bare comparison of the current bar's open and high against the prior bar's high plus a tick offset

notes: General entry hygiene rule, not specific to wedges; applies to any signal-bar breakout setup in the corpus.

candidates.name: SpikeAndChannelMinimumTargetExit
candidates.quote: As with all spike and channel patterns, the minimum target is the start of the channel, which was the high following bar 1, and there was enough room for at least a long scalp.
candidates.description: In a spike-and-channel wedge pullback, the minimum profit target for a long scalp is the price level marking the start of the channel (the extreme reached right after the spike).
candidates.pseudocode:
minTargetPrice = channelStartExtreme; // the extreme (e.g. high) of the bar marking the end of the spike / start of the channel, identified when the pattern formed
exitLongAtTarget = high[0] >= minTargetPrice
candidates.book_order_type: limit exit (or discretionary scale-out) at the channel-start price

complexity.reason: the target price itself is a stored constant once known, but identifying the spike/channel boundary requires pivot/pattern detection

notes: Spike-and-channel is likely already a shared primitive from the Trends book; not redefined here.

candidates.name: TwoLegMeasuredMoveExit
candidates.quote: traders should swing part or all of their longs from the bar 3 entry, expecting approximately a measured move up equal to about the height of the gap spike... The measured move could also be a leg 1 = leg 2 type, with bar 3 being the bottom of the second leg up.
candidates.description: For a two-legged move, project a measured-move target for the second leg equal in size to the first leg, added from the start of the second leg.
candidates.book_order_type: limit exit (or discretionary scale-out) at the measured-move price

complexity.reason: leg1/leg2 boundaries require swing-pivot identification before the arithmetic (which is itself trivial) can run

notes: Generic 'leg1 = leg2' measured move; likely recurs across many chapters as a shared primitive once pivot detection exists.

candidates.name: WedgeSlopeDeterminesBias
candidates.quote: if a wedge is sloping up and to the right, whether it is a pullback in a bear trend or a top in a bull trend, it can be thought of as a bear flag... If it is sloping down and to the right, it can be thought of as a bull flag whether it is an actual bull flag or at the bottom of a bear trend.
candidates.description: A wedge's expected breakout direction is set by its slope, independent of prior trend context: an up-sloping wedge is treated as bearish (expect a downside breakout), a down-sloping wedge as bullish (expect an upside breakout).
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (directional bias filter feeding a breakout entry)

complexity.reason: needs trend-line slope computed from detected swing pivots

candidates.name: AvoidEagerHigh2EntryAfterStrongSpike
candidates.quote: Do not be too eager to buy the high 2 after the second leg down when both the first and second pushes down have strong momentum. A strong first spike down often means that you should allow for a possible wedge correction.
candidates.description: In a wedge bull-flag setup, if both the first and second down-pushes show strong momentum, skip the eager buy at the high-2 breakout and instead wait for a pullback from the breakout above the high-2 signal bar (a second-entry setup).
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (gates whether to take the high-2 buy stop or wait for a later pullback entry)

complexity.reason: push-level 'momentum' has no stated bar test; needs a design decision (e.g., trend-bar fraction, overlap count, or bar count) before coding

rejected.quote: In general, only very experienced traders should consider placing trades in tight trading ranges because they are difficult to interpret and that lowers the odds of any successful trade.
rejected.reason: pure discretion (trader-experience gate), no bar-level test

rejected.quote: Look for short entries and don't worry too much about counting legs if those thoughts are giving you an excuse to avoid placing orders.
rejected.reason: pure discretion, explicitly advises against a mechanical test

chapter_summary: Chapter 18 defines the wedge / three-push pullback as a countertrend move of at least three swing pushes, then splits its trading logic into a with-trend wedge-flag entry (buy the reversal after the third push) versus a countertrend wedge-reversal entry (wait for a second signal unless extremely strong), plus duration heuristics (10-20 bars for flags, 20+ for reversals), a mechanical gap-avoidance rule for the breakout entry, spike-and-channel / leg1=leg2 measured-move targets, and a slope-based directional-bias classifier. The chapter is otherwise mostly nine worked chart examples (bars numbered 1-22 per figure); the general rules above were extracted from the surrounding prose, not the specific bar annotations, which the dedup pass can safely ignore.
